record.original_question: For each integer k > 2, does the Diophantine equation y = 2 x1 x2 ... xk + 1 have infinitely many solutions in prime numbers?

evidence.quote: Conjecture Let k > 2 a positive integer. The diophantine equation: y = 2 x1x2 ... xk + 1 has an infinity of solutions of primes.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $k > 2$ be a fixed integer. Determine whether there exist infinitely many $(k+1)$-tuples of prime numbers $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k, y)$ satisfying the Diophantine equation
$$y = 2\, x_1 x_2 \cdots x_k + 1,$$
i.e., whether infinitely many primes $y$ can be represented as one more than twice a product of $k$ (not necessarily distinct) primes.
artifact.status_search_result: No published resolution of this conjecture was located. The problem generalizes Sophie Germain–type questions (the $k=1$ case is the classical Sophie Germain prime conjecture, itself open) and falls within the broad class of unsolved problems about primes represented by multiplicative expressions, none of which have a known proof of infinitude. Hence the status is consistent with the problem being open.

status_evidence.title: Landau's problems - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Several conjectures on infinitude of primes of special forms remain unsolved, including Sophie Germain primes and related multiplicative-plus-one constructions.
status_evidence.claim: Closely related infinitude-of-primes conjectures (e.g., Sophie Germain primes, the k=1 case) remain open.

status_evidence.title: Patterns in Primes (K. Conrad)
status_evidence.snippet: Many natural conjectures asserting infinitely many primes of a given multiplicative form are still unproved.
status_evidence.claim: There is no known proof for infinitude of primes given by such multiplicative-plus-one forms.
